description: One small commit for man, one giant leap for coders.
summary:
EarthLens is a web app that lets anyone investigate long-term environmental change anywhere on Earth using NASA data. Users pick a location on an interactive globe, one of six variables (air temperature, relative humidity, extreme heat, precipitation, vegetation greenness or soil moisture) and a range of years. EarthLens retrieves real observations from NASA POWER, MODIS, GPM IMERG, GLDAS and SMAP.

It addresses the challenge by showing what is changing, where, how much and whether the change is statistically significant. It checks data completeness without filling gaps, estimates trends with a robust Theil–Sen slope, and tests them with Mann–Kendall, seasonal and change-point checks. Compare Lab tests the evidence itself. It compares datasets to show where they agree, and compares statistical methods on the same observations to show how analytical choices change conclusions. Every result includes a plain-language explanation, data sources and limitations. Mission Scientist, an AI assistant, answers questions using only the computed results.

This matters because simple charts can hide missing data or make weak trends look stronger than they are. EarthLens makes careful, transparent trend detection usable by students, journalists, communities and decision-makers.
details:
PROJECT DETAILS

What it does

EarthLens is a web app that lets anyone investigate long-term environmental change anywhere on Earth using NASA data, with the statistics, data quality and limitations in plain view. You pick a point on an interactive globe, choose a variable (air temperature, humidity, extreme heat, precipitation, vegetation greenness/NDVI or soil moisture) and a range of years. EarthLens retrieves the NASA data, checks completeness month by month, keeps missing data missing (nothing is interpolated or set to zero), builds one value per year, and estimates the trend with robust statistics: a Theil–Sen slope and, when there are enough years, a Mann–Kendall significance test with a serial-dependence screen. The result is explained in plain language alongside the dataset, the exact grid cell or area analysed, excluded years, uncertainty and known limitations.

Example: for Yangon, Myanmar (2015–2024, NASA POWER near-surface air temperature) the Theil–Sen slope is about +0.0205 °C per year, but the trend is not statistically significant (Mann–Kendall p = 1). EarthLens says exactly that, instead of presenting a weak trend as a conclusion.

Benefits and intended impact

NASA publishes decades of satellite and model data, but using it normally takes programming and remote-sensing expertise, and simple charts can mislead by hiding gaps or overstating weak trends. EarthLens gives students, educators, journalists, community groups and decision-makers an honest first look at local environmental trends, and teaches how to read evidence: a trend is not a cause, "no trend detected" is not "no change", and model grid cells are not ground stations.

Key features

• Interactive MapLibre globe with NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery; shareable investigations via the page URL

• Historical Discovery: annual and monthly charts, year slider and observation passport

• Mission Findings: slope, significance, eligible years and scientific guardrails

• Scientific Evaluation: valid/missing-month matrix, 95% slope interval and method notes

• Statistical Methods Lab: OLS vs Theil–Sen, autocorrelation, abrupt changes and an outlier experiment (clearly labelled simulations)

• Compare Datasets and Earth System Relationships, always descriptive and never presented as causal

• Data provenance for every result: dataset, version, spatial support, units and caveats

• Offline mode with clearly labelled saved snapshots of earlier live retrievals

• Mission Scientist assistant that explains the current investigation, grounded in its data and caveats

Tools, languages and data

Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, Recharts, MapLibre GL. Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, httpx; Docker for deployment. Data: NASA POWER API; NASA GPM IMERG, MODIS NDVI, GLDAS and SMAP via Google Earth Engine; NASA GIBS imagery. CHIRPS and ERA5-Land are used only as comparison datasets. The Mission Scientist assistant uses the Google Gemini API.

Creativity

EarthLens turns trend analysis into a guided "mission": explore, discover, review the evidence and trace it to its source. It has an original space-observatory design and team branding, and its focus is on what the data can't tell you as much as what it can.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty first: robust estimators, explicit significance caveats, never filling gaps, never mixing datasets, and labelling snapshots, simulations and correlations clearly. We also considered accessibility (reduced-motion support, colour plus shape and text cues), plain-language explanations for non-experts, dataset coverage limits, and graceful behaviour when the backend or NASA services are unavailable.

Live app: https://earthlens.psphyo.xyz

Demo video: https://youtu.be/zZR9ojx6FMY

Code: https://github.com/josephliu-4545/code-me-to-the-moon---ETSD
